questions.stem: What is the basic unit of all living things?
questions.explanation: The cell theory states that all living things are made of cells, and that cells are the smallest unit that can be called living. Atoms are smaller, but they are not alive.
questions.teaching:
Biology is organised in levels, each built from the one below, and knowing the ladder answers a lot of questions at once.

At the bottom sits the smallest unit that is genuinely alive — it can take in energy, respond to its surroundings and make copies of itself. Group many of the same type together and you get a tissue. Combine tissues into a structure with a job and you get an organ. Organs working together form a system, and systems form the whole organism. Some living things are just one of these units; you are made of roughly 30 trillion.

questions.stem: Which structure controls the activities of a eukaryotic cell and contains its DNA?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds the cell's DNA and directs the cell's activities. The membrane controls what enters and leaves, which is a different kind of control.

questions.stem: What is the job of the cell membrane?
options: Giving the cell a rigid, fixed shape
Controlling what moves into and out of the cell
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is partially permeable: it lets some substances through and blocks others. A rigid fixed shape comes from the cell wall, which only plant, fungal and bacterial cells have.

questions.stem: In which organelle does most respiration happen, releasing energy for the cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria release energy from glucose during aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts do the opposite job — they capture light energy to make glucose.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but never in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane. Animal cells have a membrane but no wall, which is why they have no fixed shape.

questions.stem: What is the jelly-like substance that fills a cell and holds the organelles?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm is the watery jelly where most chemical reactions of the cell take place. Cell sap is the liquid specifically inside a plant cell's vacuole.

questions.stem: Which pigment inside chloroplasts absorbs light for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy. Cellulose is the material of the cell wall — easy to confuse because both are found in plants.

questions.stem: Which of these is a single-celled (unicellular) organism?
questions.explanation: An amoeba carries out all life processes within one cell. Mushrooms, jellyfish and mosses are all multicellular, even though some look simple.

questions.stem: What instrument is used to see cells that are too small for the naked eye?
questions.explanation: A microscope magnifies small objects. The 'scope' names are easy to mix up: telescopes are for distant objects, stethoscopes are for listening.

questions.stem: Which structure in a plant cell stores water and cell sap, and helps keep the cell firm?
questions.explanation: A plant cell's large permanent vacuole fills with cell sap and pushes outwards on the cell wall, keeping the cell firm. Animal cells have only small temporary vacuoles, if any.

questions.stem: Where are proteins made inside a cell?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins. Mitochondria supply the energy for that work, but they do not build the proteins themselves.
questions.teaching:
Each organelle does a specific job, and matching structure to job is what most cell questions come down to.

Mitochondria release energy from glucose. Chloroplasts capture light energy in plants. The nucleus stores the instructions. The vacuole stores water and keeps a plant cell firm. And one very small structure, found in enormous numbers in every cell including bacteria, reads those instructions and assembles amino acids into chains — that is where proteins get built. Cells that produce a lot of protein, such as those in the pancreas, are packed with them.

questions.stem: Which of these do bacterial cells NOT have?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm rather than inside a nucleus. They still have DNA, a membrane and cytoplasm.
questions.teaching:
Cells come in two broad kinds, and the difference is about internal organisation rather than size alone.

One kind keeps its DNA inside a membrane-bound compartment and has several other compartments doing specialised jobs — this is what animal, plant and fungal cells look like. The other kind is much smaller and simpler: its DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm as a single loop, with no membrane-bound compartments at all. Bacteria are the second kind. They still have a membrane, a cell wall and ribosomes, so it is only the compartments that are missing.

questions.stem: What does the cell wall of a plant cell provide?
options: Control of what enters the cell
questions.explanation: The cellulose cell wall is strong and rigid, so it supports the cell and holds its shape. Controlling entry is the membrane's job — the wall is fully permeable.

questions.stem: A group of similar cells working together to do the same job is called:
questions.explanation: The order is cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. A tissue is the first level up from a single cell.

questions.stem: Which two structures are found in plant cells but not animal cells?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts (plus a large vacuole) as well as everything an animal cell has. Every other structure listed is common to both.

questions.stem: What is magnification on a microscope?
options: How thick the specimen on the slide is
How many times larger the image is than the real object
How clear and sharp the image is
How bright the light shining through the slide is
questions.explanation: Magnification is the number of times bigger the image appears. How clear and sharp it is is called resolution — a magnified but blurry image is not useful.

questions.stem: Which type of cell has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles?
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells, including bacteria, do not.

questions.stem: What is the correct name for the structures inside a cell that each do a particular job?
questions.explanation: Organelles are the small structures inside a single cell. Organs are much larger structures made of many tissues — the similar names are the trap here.

questions.stem: Which process do chloroplasts carry out?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts use light energy to make glucose in photosynthesis. Respiration, which releases that energy again, happens in mitochondria.
questions.teaching:
Chloroplasts are found in plant cells and not in animal cells, and their green colour is the clue to what they do.

That colour comes from chlorophyll, a pigment that absorbs light energy. The organelle uses that captured energy to combine carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product. So it is where light energy is converted into chemical energy the plant can store and use. Do not confuse it with respiration, which happens in mitochondria and runs the other way — breaking glucose down to release energy, in plants and animals alike.

questions.stem: Why are onion cells often used in school microscope work?
options: Onion cells are much larger than any other plant cells
Onion cells are the only plant cells with a visible nucleus
Onion cells do not need to be stained to be seen
A single layer can be peeled off, so light passes through it
questions.explanation: The thin epidermis peels away as a layer one cell thick, so light passes through and the cells are visible. Staining with iodine still helps show the nuclei.

questions.stem: A student looks at a cell under a microscope and sees a cell wall, a nucleus and no chloroplasts. What is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Root cells are plant cells, so they have a wall and a nucleus, but they are underground and get no light, so they have no chloroplasts. A bacterial cell would have no nucleus.

questions.stem: A cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no cell wall made of cellulose. What is it?
questions.explanation: The absence of a nucleus points to a prokaryote. Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose, and bacteria have no mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why do muscle cells contain far more mitochondria than fat storage cells?
options: Muscle cells store more DNA than fat cells
Mitochondria help muscle cells stay a fixed shape
Muscle cells need to release much more energy to contract
Muscle cells are larger, so they need more of every organelle
questions.explanation: Mitochondria release energy by respiration, and contracting muscle is energy-hungry. Cell size alone does not decide organelle numbers — the cell's job does.

questions.stem: A red blood cell has no nucleus. What is the advantage of this?
options: The cell can change into other cell types
There is more room to carry oxygen
The cell can divide much faster
The cell can survive without any energy
questions.explanation: Losing the nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen. It is a trade-off: without a nucleus the cell cannot divide and only lasts about 120 days.

questions.stem: Root hair cells have a long, thin extension into the soil. Which function does this shape support?
questions.explanation: The extension increases the surface area in contact with soil water, so absorption is faster. Root hair cells are below ground and have no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise.

questions.stem: A student calculates that an image is 100 times bigger than the real cell. What have they worked out?
questions.explanation: 'How many times bigger' is magnification. Resolution is about detail, and field of view is how much of the slide you can see at once.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why cells are so small?
options: A small cell has a large surface area compared with its volume, so substances move in and out quickly
Small cells contain fewer organelles, so they need less energy
Small cells are harder for predators to attack
Small cells can hold more DNA for their size
questions.explanation: As a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area, so the membrane cannot supply the inside fast enough. Staying small keeps that ratio high.

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a cell appears green under low power. Which organelle is responsible?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll, and there are enough of them to colour the whole cell. Mitochondria are colourless and too small to see at low power.

questions.stem: A plant is left without water and its leaves go limp. At the cell level, what has happened?
options: The chloroplasts have stopped photosynthesising, so cells collapsed
The nuclei have shrunk, making the cells smaller
The vacuoles have lost water, so the cells no longer push against their walls
questions.explanation: Firm plant tissue depends on full vacuoles pressing outwards on the cell walls. Lose the water and the cells go flaccid, which is what wilting is. The walls themselves are still there.

questions.stem: Which of these is arranged in the correct order, smallest to largest?
questions.explanation: Organelles are parts of a cell, so they come first. Then cells group into tissues, and tissues into organs.

questions.stem: Why is a very thin specimen needed for a light microscope?
options: Light has to pass through the specimen to form the image
Thick specimens are too heavy for the stage
questions.explanation: A light microscope shines light up through the slide, so anything too thick blocks it and the image is dark. Thickness does not change how large the cells actually are.

questions.stem: A cell is described as prokaryotic. Which structure will it definitely NOT have?
questions.explanation: 'Prokaryotic' means 'before the nucleus'. Prokaryotes do have ribosomes, cytoplasm and a membrane — the missing feature is the nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.

questions.stem: Sperm cells have many mitochondria packed behind the head. Why?
options: To store extra DNA to pass on
To help the sperm cell digest the egg
To keep the sperm cell a fixed shape
To supply energy for the tail to move the cell
questions.explanation: Swimming takes continuous energy, which mitochondria release by respiration. The DNA is carried in the head's nucleus, not in mitochondria.

questions.stem: A student stains onion cells with iodine. What does the stain make easier to see?
questions.explanation: Iodine binds to material in the nucleus, making it stand out against the pale cytoplasm. The cellulose walls are already visible unstained, and mitochondria and individual DNA molecules are far too small to resolve with a school microscope.

questions.stem: Which of these cells would you expect to have the most chloroplasts?
options: A cell in the middle of a tree trunk
A cell lining a flower's nectar tube
A palisade cell near the top of a leaf
questions.explanation: Palisade cells sit just under the leaf surface where light is strongest, so they are packed with chloroplasts. Roots and trunk interiors receive no light.

questions.stem: Nerve cells are long and thin, sometimes over a metre. Which function does this support?
options: Carrying electrical signals over long distances
Absorbing more nutrients from the blood
Dividing more often than other cells
questions.explanation: A long fibre lets one cell carry a signal from, say, the spinal cord to the foot without handing over between cells. Mature nerve cells actually divide very rarely.

questions.stem: Two students argue about whether a virus is a cell. Which reason correctly settles it?
options: A virus is a cell, because it contains genetic material
A virus is a cell, because it can reproduce
A virus is not a cell, because it is too small to be seen
A virus is not a cell, because it has no cytoplasm, membrane-bound organelles or ability to respire
questions.explanation: Having genetic material is not enough — a virus has no cytoplasm and carries out no life processes of its own, so it fails the cell definition. Size alone is not the reason; bacteria are tiny too.

questions.stem: Why can a single-celled organism survive without any organs?
options: It absorbs organs from other organisms
It is too small to need to move or feed
One cell carries out all the life processes itself
questions.explanation: In a unicellular organism, one cell does everything: feeding, respiring, removing waste and reproducing. It still needs energy and still moves.

questions.stem: A leaf cell has fewer chloroplasts than expected. Which observation would best explain it?
options: The leaf was picked in the morning
The leaf came from a large plant
The leaf was thicker than usual
The leaf grew in deep shade
questions.explanation: Chloroplast numbers respond to light available during growth. Time of picking and plant size do not change how many chloroplasts a cell built.

questions.stem: A cell is 0.05 mm wide. Under a microscope its image measures 10 mm. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 10 ÷ 0.05 = 200. Dividing the wrong way round gives 0.005, and mixing up units is the usual source of ×50 or ×500.

questions.stem: Why does the cell theory say all cells come from existing cells, rather than forming from non-living material?
options: Because DNA cannot be made outside a cell
Experiments such as Pasteur's showed that sealed sterilised broth grew no organisms until cells entered it
Because no one has ever built a cell in a laboratory
Because cells are too complicated to form by chance
questions.explanation: The claim rests on experimental evidence: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment showed growth only appeared when cells could reach the broth. The other statements are assertions, not evidence.

questions.stem: An electron microscope can resolve structures a light microscope cannot, even at the same magnification. Why?
options: Electron microscopes magnify many more times
Electron beams have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
Electron microscopes shine a much brighter light
questions.explanation: Resolution is limited by wavelength: light waves cannot distinguish detail finer than about half their wavelength. Electrons have far shorter wavelengths, so finer detail is resolved. Extra magnification without extra resolution just gives a bigger blur.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell doubles in length along each edge. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area scales with length squared (×4) and volume with length cubed (×8), so the ratio changes by 4/8 — it halves. This is exactly why cells divide instead of growing indefinitely.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the idea that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
options: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and divide independently of the cell
Mitochondria are found in all eukaryotic cells
Mitochondria release energy, as bacteria do
Mitochondria are about the same size as a nucleus
questions.explanation: Their own circular DNA and independent division are bacteria-like features that a normal organelle would not have. Being present everywhere or releasing energy does not point to a bacterial origin, and mitochondria are much smaller than a nucleus.

questions.stem: A student claims a plant cell would burst if placed in pure water, like an animal cell does. Why is this wrong?
options: The rigid cell wall resists the pressure as water enters
Plant cells do not take in water by osmosis
The vacuole absorbs all the extra water permanently
Chloroplasts remove excess water during photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Water does enter a plant cell by osmosis, but the cellulose wall pushes back, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting. An animal cell has no wall, so it can burst.

questions.stem: Specialised cells in one organism all contain the same DNA. How can they look and behave so differently?
options: The DNA changes as the organism grows older
Different genes are switched on in different cell types
Each cell type loses the genes it does not need
Each cell type has a different number of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Cells differentiate by expressing different subsets of the same genome. They keep the full set of genes — losing them would make the cell unable to divide into anything else.

questions.stem: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
questions.explanation: Total magnification is the product of the two lenses: 10 × 40 = 400. Adding them, which gives 50, is the most common error.

questions.stem: Which observation would most strongly challenge the claim that all living things are made of cells?
options: Finding a cell without a nucleus
Finding an organism made of only one cell
Finding a cell too small to see with a light microscope
Finding an organism that grows, reproduces and respires without any cells
questions.explanation: A theory is challenged by a case that contradicts it. Cells without nuclei, single-celled organisms and very small cells are all already known and fit the theory perfectly well.

questions.stem: Which organelle is sometimes called the site of aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose, and it takes place in mitochondria.

questions.stem: What is a specialised cell?
options: A cell found only in plants
A cell with a structure suited to one particular job
A cell that is larger than normal
A cell that can turn into any other cell
questions.explanation: Specialised cells have adaptations that fit one function, like a red blood cell's disc shape. A cell that can become any type is a stem cell, which is the opposite idea.

questions.stem: Which part of a microscope do you look through?
questions.explanation: The eyepiece (ocular lens) is at the top. The objective lenses sit above the specimen, and the stage is the platform the slide rests on.

questions.stem: What holds the slide in place on a microscope?
questions.explanation: Stage clips grip the slide so it does not slide around while you focus.

questions.stem: Which type of organism is made of many cells?
questions.explanation: 'Multi' means many. Unicellular organisms are made of one cell, and viruses are not made of cells at all.

questions.stem: What is the outer boundary of an animal cell called?
questions.explanation: Animal cells are bounded by a cell membrane only. The nuclear membrane is inside, around the nucleus.

questions.stem: What is stored inside a plant cell's vacuole?
options: Cell sap, which is mostly water with dissolved substances
questions.explanation: Cell sap is a watery solution of sugars, salts and pigments. Chlorophyll is in chloroplasts and DNA is in the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an organelle?
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of cells, so it is bigger than a cell, not a part of one.
questions.teaching:
An organelle is a specialised structure *inside* a single cell, each with its own job — a tiny organ for the cell, which is where the name comes from.

The list includes the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts in plants, and the vacuole. All of them fit inside one cell. So the test for this question is scale: anything larger than a single cell cannot be one, however important it is. Something made of many cells working together has moved up a level of organisation entirely, and that is the odd one out here.

questions.stem: What does 'partially permeable' mean when describing a cell membrane?
options: It only lets water out, never in
It lets some substances through but not others
questions.explanation: Partially (or selectively) permeable membranes are choosy. A fully permeable barrier, like a plant cell wall, lets everything small through.

questions.stem: Which structure contains the genetic instructions for making proteins?
questions.explanation: DNA carries the instructions. Ribosomes read a copy of those instructions to build proteins.

questions.stem: About how many cells is an adult human made of?
questions.explanation: Estimates put an adult human at roughly 30-40 trillion cells. The scale is one of the reasons cells must be microscopic.

questions.stem: What are yeast cells an example of?
questions.explanation: Yeasts are fungi made of one cell. They have a nucleus and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Which structure would you look for to confirm a cell is eukaryotic?
questions.explanation: All cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. Only eukaryotes have a nucleus.

questions.stem: What is the correct name for a cell's internal skeleton of protein fibres?
questions.explanation: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that supports the cell and moves things around inside it.

questions.stem: Why are stains such as methylene blue used in microscopy?
options: They add contrast so structures are easier to see
They kill bacteria on the slide
questions.explanation: Most cell contents are colourless and nearly transparent. A stain darkens certain structures so they stand out.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes cytoplasm?
options: A watery jelly where most of a cell's reactions happen
A rigid layer that supports the cell
A store of the cell's genetic material
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm is the fluid interior. Support comes from the wall, DNA is in the nucleus, light capture is in chloroplasts.

questions.stem: What happens to a cell's DNA before the cell divides?
questions.explanation: DNA is copied so each new cell gets a full set. Halving happens only in the special division that makes sex cells.

questions.stem: Which cells in a leaf let gases move in and out?
questions.explanation: Guard cells open and close the stomata, the pores gases pass through. Palisade cells do the photosynthesis behind them.

questions.stem: What is a cell that has not yet specialised called?
questions.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialised and can develop into different cell types.

questions.stem: Which organelle is present in large numbers in a cell that is very active?
questions.explanation: Active cells need lots of energy, and mitochondria release it. Most cells have only one nucleus no matter how active they are.

questions.stem: Why does a leaf look green but a carrot root does not?
options: Carrot cells have no cell walls
Leaf cells are larger than carrot cells
Leaf cells contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll; root cells do not
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll gives the green colour, and chloroplasts only develop in cells that receive light. Roots grow in the dark.

questions.stem: A student sees moving structures inside a plant cell under the microscope. What are they most likely watching?
options: Bacteria that have infected the cell
Chloroplasts being carried around by streaming cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Cytoplasmic streaming carries chloroplasts around the cell, which is visible at school magnifications. Nuclear division and molecular-level events are not.

questions.stem: Which pair of cells would look most similar under a microscope?
options: An onion cell and a bacterial cell
A bacterial cell and a human liver cell
A human cheek cell and a human liver cell
A human cheek cell and an onion cell
questions.explanation: Both cheek and liver cells are animal cells: membrane, nucleus, no wall, no chloroplasts. The other pairs cross between kingdoms or between prokaryote and eukaryote.

questions.stem: Why must a cell that has grown large either divide or stop growing?
options: It uses up all the water in the cytoplasm
Its surface area becomes too small to supply its volume
Its nucleus runs out of DNA
questions.explanation: Volume grows faster than surface area, so the membrane eventually cannot move materials in and out fast enough. This applies to animal cells with no wall too.

questions.stem: A cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution and shrinks. What has moved, and which way?
options: Water has moved out of the cell
Sugar has moved out of the cell
Water has moved into the cell
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated — out of the cell here. The membrane blocks most of the sugar.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that yeast cells are alive rather than just particles?
options: They are roughly round in shape
They reproduce and produce carbon dioxide when fed sugar
They can be seen under a microscope
questions.explanation: Reproducing and respiring are life processes. Being visible, round or buoyant are properties non-living particles have too.

questions.stem: A biologist finds a cell with a wall but no nucleus and no mitochondria. Which group does it belong to?
questions.explanation: The absence of a nucleus rules out plants, fungi and animals, all of which are eukaryotes. Bacteria have a wall but no nucleus.

questions.stem: Why can a light microscope not show individual ribosomes?
options: They are only present in dead cells
They are smaller than the resolution limit of visible light
They are transparent and cannot be stained
They move too quickly to be seen
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are around 20 nanometres — far below what light waves can resolve. An electron microscope is needed.

questions.stem: Which change would let a cell absorb substances faster without getting bigger overall?
options: Folding the membrane into many small projections
questions.explanation: Folds and microvilli increase surface area without increasing volume much. Thickening the membrane or adding a wall would slow absorption, not speed it.

questions.stem: A student writes 'plant cells have no mitochondria because they have chloroplasts'. What is wrong?
options: Plant cells do not need energy
Plant cells have both — they respire as well as photosynthesise
Plant cells have mitochondria but no chloroplasts
Chloroplasts and mitochondria are the same organelle
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; respiration releases it again. Plants do both, day and night, so they need mitochondria too.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes how a specialised tissue forms?
options: Stem cells divide, then differentiate into cells of the same type that group together
Organelles group together to form a tissue
questions.explanation: Cells come first: they divide, specialise, and similar ones group into tissues. Organs are built from tissues, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Under low power a student sees a whole layer of cells; under high power only two or three. Why?
options: Higher magnification shows a smaller field of view
The cells have moved off the slide
questions.explanation: Field of view shrinks as magnification rises — you see less area but in more detail. This is why you always find the specimen on low power first.

questions.stem: Which feature of a palisade cell is a direct adaptation for photosynthesis?
options: Being packed with chloroplasts and box-shaped so many fit near the surface
Having a thick cell wall for strength
questions.explanation: Chloroplast density and tight packing near the lit surface both serve photosynthesis. Palisade cells do have a vacuole, and wall thickness is not the point here.

questions.stem: Why is a cheek cell smear better than a thick scraping for microscope work?
options: A single layer lets light through so individual cells can be seen
A thick scraping dries out before it can be examined
A single layer needs no coverslip
questions.explanation: Cells piled on top of each other block light and overlap in the image. Spreading them thin separates them.

questions.stem: A cell contains chloroplasts, a cell wall and a large vacuole. Which is the strongest conclusion?
options: It is a plant cell, since only plant cells have all three of these
It is an animal cell with unusual organelles
questions.explanation: All three features together occur only in plant cells. Fungi have walls and vacuoles but never chloroplasts, and animal cells have none of the three.

questions.stem: What is the main reason multicellular organisms can grow much larger than unicellular ones?
options: Their cells are individually much bigger
They do not need to exchange materials with their surroundings
Their cells have more DNA each
Their cells specialise, so different cells handle different jobs
questions.explanation: Specialisation and division of labour, including transport systems, let the body grow beyond what one cell could supply. Individual cell size stays roughly the same.

questions.stem: Which of these would you expect a cell lining the small intestine to have?
options: No mitochondria, because absorption needs no energy
Many folds on its surface to absorb nutrients faster
Chloroplasts to make its own food
questions.explanation: Microvilli increase the absorbing surface. Absorption often needs energy, so these cells are rich in mitochondria, not short of them.

questions.stem: Why do biologists describe the cell as the 'basic unit of life' rather than the atom?
options: A cell is the smallest thing that carries out all the processes of life
Atoms are not found in living things
Cells are the smallest things that exist
Atoms are too large to fit inside organisms
questions.explanation: Atoms are the building blocks of matter, living or not, and cannot respire, grow or reproduce on their own. The cell is the smallest unit that can.

questions.stem: A microscope image is blurry at high power. Which adjustment is most likely to help?
options: Using the coarse focus knob at full turn
questions.explanation: Fine focus makes the tiny adjustments high power needs. Coarse focus at high power risks driving the objective into the slide.

questions.stem: A cell is 20 micrometres across. How many would fit end to end across 1 millimetre?
questions.explanation: There are 1000 micrometres in a millimetre, so 1000 ÷ 20 = 50. Losing track of the 1000 factor gives 20 or 5.

questions.stem: Why is it more accurate to say the nucleus 'stores and issues instructions' than 'controls everything'?
options: Many cell activities are regulated by conditions in the cytoplasm and at the membrane too
The nucleus senses conditions outside the cell and responds directly
Cells with no nucleus are not alive
questions.explanation: Regulation is distributed: signals at the membrane and chemistry in the cytoplasm both shape what a cell does. The nucleus is central but not the sole controller.

questions.stem: Which comparison correctly contrasts a plant cell and an animal cell in pure water?
options: The plant cell bursts; the animal cell becomes turgid
Neither cell takes in any water
The plant cell becomes turgid; the animal cell may burst
questions.explanation: Both take in water by osmosis, but only the plant cell has a wall to resist the pressure, so it becomes firm instead of rupturing.

questions.stem: A drug stops ribosomes from working. What is the most direct effect on a cell?
options: It can no longer release energy
It can no longer copy its DNA
It can no longer make proteins
questions.explanation: Ribosomes assemble proteins, so protein synthesis stops first. Energy release and DNA copying fail later, once the proteins that carry them out run out.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that all cells come from pre-existing cells?
options: Cells have been observed dividing to produce new cells
Cells are all roughly the same size
Cells cannot be seen without a microscope
questions.explanation: Direct observation of division is the evidence. Shared features like DNA are consistent with the claim but do not demonstrate where new cells come from.

questions.stem: A cell has a very large surface area to volume ratio. What does this suggest about it?
options: It will have very few mitochondria
Exchange with its surroundings will be efficient
It must be a very large cell
It cannot survive without a cell wall
questions.explanation: A high ratio means plenty of membrane per unit of interior, so materials move in and out quickly. Large cells have the opposite — a low ratio.

questions.stem: Why do scientists classify mitochondria and chloroplasts as semi-autonomous organelles?
options: Each has its own DNA and can divide within the cell
Each can survive outside the cell
Each can leave and re-enter the cell
Each is found only in plants
questions.explanation: Their own DNA and ability to divide give them partial independence — 'semi'. Neither can survive alone outside the cell.

questions.stem: A student concludes a specimen is a plant because it has a cell wall. Why is that unsafe?
options: Fungi and bacteria also have cell walls, though made of different materials
Plant cells do not have cell walls
Cell walls only appear after staining
questions.explanation: Cell walls are found in plants, fungi, bacteria and algae. Chloroplasts, not the wall alone, are the reliable plant indicator.

questions.stem: An image of a cell is 60 mm wide at ×300 magnification. How wide is the real cell?
questions.explanation: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 60 ÷ 300 = 0.2 mm. Multiplying instead of dividing is the usual mistake.

questions.stem: Which statement about cell theory is a limitation rather than a strength?
options: It explains where new cells come from
It does not readily account for viruses, which have genetic material but no cells
It applies to both plants and animals
It is supported by microscope observations
questions.explanation: Viruses sit awkwardly against a theory built around cells — a genuine boundary case. The other options are all reasons the theory is well supported.

questions.stem: Who was the first person to use the word 'cell' for what he saw in cork?
questions.explanation: Hooke looked at cork through an early microscope in 1665 and named the boxes 'cells' because they reminded him of monks' rooms.

questions.stem: Who first observed living single-celled organisms, which he called 'animalcules'?
questions.explanation: Van Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses and was the first to describe living microorganisms in pond water and other samples.

questions.stem: What are the three parts of the cell theory?
options: Cells respire; cells reproduce; cells move
All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; cells come from existing cells
All cells are the same size; cells contain DNA; cells can be seen with a microscope
Cells make tissues; tissues make organs; organs make organisms
questions.explanation: Those three statements are the cell theory. The organisation sequence and the life processes are true, but they are not what the theory states.

questions.stem: What does an organ system do?
options: A structure inside a single cell
A group of organs working together on one major function
A group of cells of the same type
questions.explanation: For example, the digestive system is several organs working together. A group of the same cells is a tissue.

questions.stem: Which of these is a tissue?
questions.explanation: Muscle is many similar cells working together. The heart is an organ made of several tissues, and the circulatory system is a system of organs.
questions.teaching:
The levels of organisation are the key here: cell, tissue, organ, system, organism.

A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on one job — not a single cell, and not a whole structure made of several different tissues. So think about what each option actually is. Something made of one cell type doing one job sits at the tissue level. Something combining several tissues into a working unit, like a stomach or a leaf, has moved up to the organ level. Blood, bone, muscle and nerve are the standard tissue examples in animals.

questions.stem: What does an amoeba use to move and surround food?
options: Extensions of its cytoplasm called pseudopodia
questions.explanation: An amoeba flows forward by pushing out pseudopodia ('false feet'), which also engulf food particles.

questions.stem: Which structure lets a sperm cell swim?
questions.explanation: The flagellum whips back and forth to drive the cell forward.
questions.teaching:
Specialised cells have shapes that fit their job, and sperm cells are the standard example of the principle.

A sperm cell has to travel a considerable distance to reach an egg, so it needs a way to propel itself. It also carries many mitochondria packed just behind the head, supplying the energy that movement demands, and an enzyme package at the tip for getting through the egg's outer layer. Look at any specialised cell and ask what job it has to do — a red blood cell's disc shape, a root hair cell's long extension and a nerve cell's length all follow the same logic.

questions.stem: What shape is a red blood cell?
options: A flattened disc dented on both sides
questions.explanation: The biconcave disc shape increases surface area for absorbing oxygen and lets the cell squeeze through narrow capillaries.

questions.stem: Which cells carry water up through a plant?
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards. Phloem carries dissolved sugars around the plant.

questions.stem: What is diffusion?
options: The movement of water only, through a membrane
The active pumping of particles using energy
The splitting of one cell into two
The spreading of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive spreading down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is the special case involving water and a membrane.

questions.stem: What is osmosis?
options: The movement of any particle across a membrane
The movement of oxygen into the lungs
The breakdown of glucose to release energy
The movement of water across a partially permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Osmosis is specifically about water crossing a partially permeable membrane. Other particles moving is diffusion.

questions.stem: What is produced when a cell divides once by ordinary cell division?
questions.explanation: Ordinary division produces two cells with the same genetic material. Four cells at once is the result of the special division that makes sex cells.

questions.stem: Which organelle would be missing from a cell that cannot photosynthesise?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis needs chloroplasts. Every living cell still needs mitochondria, ribosomes and a membrane.

questions.stem: What does 'organelle' literally mean?
questions.explanation: The '-elle' ending means small — an organelle is a small structure with a job, like a tiny organ within the cell.

questions.stem: Which two life processes must every living cell carry out?
questions.explanation: Every cell respires and must get rid of waste. Only cells with chloroplasts photosynthesise, and not every cell reproduces.

questions.stem: A student wants to compare the sizes of two cells. What do they need as well as the images?
options: The time of day the slides were made
The magnification each image was taken at
The colour of the stain used
questions.explanation: Image size alone is meaningless without magnification: a small cell at high power can look bigger than a large cell at low power.

questions.stem: Why do cells in the same organism sometimes look completely different?
options: They have specialised for different functions
questions.explanation: Specialisation shapes cells to their jobs even though they share the same DNA.

questions.stem: Which explains why a plant wilts in hot weather but recovers after watering?
options: The vacuole is replaced with air and then refilled
Cells lose water and go flaccid, then refill and become turgid again
The cell walls stretch and then contract again
Chloroplasts stop photosynthesising until water returns
questions.explanation: Firmness in plant tissue comes from water pressure inside the cells pushing on their walls. It is fully reversible if the plant is watered in time.

questions.stem: A pondweed leaf is examined and gas bubbles appear in bright light. Which organelle is responsible?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis in chloroplasts produces oxygen, which comes off as bubbles in water. Respiration continues too, but the net output in bright light is oxygen.

questions.stem: Which structure most limits how fast a large animal cell can take in oxygen?
options: The surface area of its cell membrane
questions.explanation: Oxygen enters by diffusion across the membrane, so membrane area sets the rate. Cells with high demand increase that area or stay small.

questions.stem: Why is a cell wall described as fully permeable while a membrane is partially permeable?
options: The wall carries a charge, so it attracts only certain particles
The membrane is made of cellulose
The wall's open mesh lets dissolved substances pass; the membrane selects what crosses
The wall is thinner than the membrane
questions.explanation: The cellulose wall is a rigid open mesh that does not filter. Selection happens at the membrane just inside it.

questions.stem: A student says bacteria are simply very small animal cells. Give the best correction.
options: Bacteria are larger than animal cells
Bacteria have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, so they are a different type of cell
questions.explanation: The prokaryote/eukaryote difference is structural, not just a matter of size.

questions.stem: Which observation would suggest a cell is adapted for producing and exporting a lot of protein?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes make proteins, so a protein-exporting cell is packed with them along with the membranes that process and package proteins.

questions.stem: In a food-colouring-in-water demonstration, the colour spreads without stirring. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: Particles spread from high to low concentration on their own. No membrane is involved, so it is not osmosis.

questions.stem: Why does a potato chip left in salty water become floppy?
options: Salt enters the cells and dissolves the walls
The cells respire faster and use up their water
The cell membranes become fully permeable
Water leaves its cells by osmosis, so they lose turgor
questions.explanation: The salty solution has a lower water concentration, so water moves out of the cells and they go flaccid.

questions.stem: Which order of steps is correct when using a light microscope?
options: Start on the lowest power, focus with coarse then fine, then switch to higher power
Start on the highest power and use coarse focus
Focus with fine focus first, then coarse focus
Switch to high power before placing the slide
questions.explanation: Finding the specimen on low power first is what makes high power usable, and it avoids driving the objective into the slide.

questions.stem: A cell has been described as 'differentiated'. What does that mean?
options: It contains different DNA from other cells
It has developed features that suit one particular job
questions.explanation: Differentiation is the process of becoming specialised. It generally does not change the DNA present.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a cell to its adaptation?
options: Nerve cell — thick wall for support
Palisade cell — no chloroplasts, so light passes through
Root hair cell — long extension for absorbing water
Red blood cell — many mitochondria for energy
questions.explanation: The root hair's extension increases absorbing surface. Red blood cells have very few mitochondria, nerve cells have no wall, and palisade cells are full of chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Why can't most human cells survive on their own outside the body?
options: They depend on other cells for oxygen, nutrients and waste removal
They contain no DNA of their own
questions.explanation: Specialisation means a trade-off: doing one job well leaves a cell reliant on the rest of the body for everything else.

questions.stem: Which measurement would you record to compare how fast two cells respire?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen, so oxygen use per unit time is a direct measure of rate.

questions.stem: A slide shows cells joined in a single layer with no gaps. Which level of organisation is visible?
questions.explanation: Similar cells joined and working together are a tissue. An organ would show several different tissue types.

questions.stem: Why is 'bigger magnification is always better' poor microscope advice?
options: High magnification changes the specimen's real size
Beyond the resolution limit you get a larger but no more detailed image
questions.explanation: Empty magnification enlarges without adding detail. Resolution, set by wavelength and lens quality, is what limits useful magnification.

questions.stem: A cell's membrane is damaged so it can no longer control what enters. What is the most immediate consequence?
options: Its internal conditions drift towards those of its surroundings
questions.explanation: The membrane maintains a different internal environment. Lose that control and concentrations inside and outside equalise, which the cell's chemistry cannot survive.

questions.stem: Why does a multicellular organism need a transport system while an amoeba does not?
options: An amoeba has a transport system inside its nucleus
Large organisms do not need oxygen
Diffusion alone is too slow across the distances inside a large body
Multicellular organisms do not use diffusion at all
questions.explanation: Diffusion is fast over micrometres and hopeless over centimetres. An amoeba is small enough that diffusion reaches every part of it.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by finding the same organelles in plant, animal and fungal cells?
options: These groups share a common ancestor that already had those organelles
Organelles form spontaneously in any cell
These groups cannot be told apart
questions.explanation: Shared complex features across groups point to shared ancestry. The groups remain clearly distinguishable by the features they do not share.

questions.stem: A stain binds only to DNA. Which structures would light up in a plant cell?
options: The nucleus, and faintly the mitochondria and chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Most DNA is in the nucleus, but mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small DNA loops — which is itself evidence of their bacterial origins.

questions.stem: Why is a cheek cell a better choice than a nerve cell for a first look at animal cells?
options: Cheek cells are easy to collect, roughly uniform and one layer thick when smeared
Cheek cells are the only animal cells with a nucleus
Nerve cells have cell walls that block light
Cheek cells are much larger than nerve cells
questions.explanation: Practicality decides it: cheek cells are simple to obtain and prepare. Nerve cells are long, branched and embedded in tissue.

questions.stem: A cell doubles in every dimension. By what factor does its volume increase?
questions.explanation: Volume scales with the cube of length: 2³ = 8. Surface area scales with the square, ×4 — which is exactly why the ratio falls.

questions.stem: What is the name for the process by which a cell releases energy from glucose?
questions.explanation: Respiration releases energy from glucose. Photosynthesis is the reverse: it stores energy in glucose.

questions.stem: Which structure surrounds the nucleus?
questions.explanation: A nuclear membrane (envelope) keeps the DNA separate from the cytoplasm — the defining feature of eukaryotic cells.

questions.stem: What is the plural of 'nucleus'?
questions.explanation: Latin-derived biology terms often change ending in the plural: nucleus becomes nuclei, as mitochondrion becomes mitochondria.
questions.teaching:
English has borrowed a great deal of scientific vocabulary directly from Latin and Greek, and those words often keep their original plural forms.

The pattern worth learning here is that Latin words ending in -us frequently take -i in the plural: fungus becomes fungi, cactus becomes cacti, stimulus becomes stimuli. Words ending in -um usually take -a: bacterium becomes bacteria, datum becomes data. And words ending in -is take -es: hypothesis becomes hypotheses, analysis becomes analyses. Getting these right matters in written work, and 'a bacteria' is the error examiners notice most.

questions.stem: Which unit is used to measure the size of most cells?
questions.explanation: Most cells are tens of micrometres across. A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre.

questions.stem: Which of these is found in both a plant cell and a bacterial cell?
questions.explanation: Both have a cell wall, though made of different materials. Bacteria have no nucleus, chloroplasts or large vacuole.

questions.stem: A student measures 12 cells spanning the field of view, which is 1.2 mm wide. What is the average cell width?
questions.explanation: 1.2 mm ÷ 12 = 0.1 mm per cell. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 14.4 mm, which would be a visible cell.

questions.stem: Why does a cell need both a membrane and, in plants, a wall?
options: The membrane controls what crosses; the wall provides support
Both control what crosses, for extra safety
The wall controls what crosses; the membrane provides support
Only one of them is actually needed
questions.explanation: They do different jobs. The wall is fully permeable and structural; the membrane is selective.

questions.stem: Which would be strongest evidence that a sample contains living cells rather than dead ones?
options: Being able to stain the sample
Observing cytoplasmic streaming or cell division
questions.explanation: Movement and division are activities only living cells perform. Structures like walls and pigments persist after death.

questions.stem: Why does the human body contain many different cell types rather than one general type?
options: Different cell types contain different DNA
One cell type would be too large
Cells change type randomly as the body grows
Specialised cells perform particular jobs far more efficiently
questions.explanation: Division of labour is the advantage. All the cell types share the same DNA — they differ in which genes are active.

questions.stem: A slide is prepared without a coverslip. What problem is most likely?
options: The specimen dries out and the objective lens can touch the sample
The cells become too large to see
questions.explanation: A coverslip holds the specimen flat, keeps it moist and protects the lens. It does not change magnification.

questions.stem: Which cell feature would suggest the cell is adapted for storage rather than activity?
options: A large space filled with stored material and few mitochondria
questions.explanation: Storage cells devote volume to the stored substance and need little energy. Mitochondria, extensions and flagella all point to activity.

questions.stem: Why does a bacterial cell not need a transport system inside it?
options: It does not use any nutrients
It has a cell wall that moves substances
It has mitochondria to deliver materials
It is small enough for diffusion to reach every part quickly
questions.explanation: At bacterial scale, diffusion is fast enough. Bacteria have no mitochondria at all.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason plant cells can be firm without a skeleton?
options: Chloroplasts press outwards against the cell wall
Plant cell membranes are much thicker
Water pressure inside each cell pushes against its rigid wall
The cell membrane hardens once the cell is full
questions.explanation: Turgor pressure acting against the cellulose wall supports the plant. Losing the water is what makes a plant wilt.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to see the internal structure of a mitochondrion. What should they use?
options: A stained slide under low power
A light microscope on high power
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial internal structure is far below the resolution of light microscopy, however much you magnify.

questions.stem: Which statement about cell division in a growing organism is correct?
options: Existing cells simply get larger, and no new cells form
New cells come from the bloodstream
New cells are produced by existing cells dividing
New cells form spontaneously from nutrients
questions.explanation: Growth involves both cell division and cell enlargement, but every new cell comes from an existing one — the third part of cell theory.

questions.stem: Why is it misleading to say a cell membrane is 'like a wall with gates'?
options: The membrane is fluid and its transport proteins move within it, unlike a fixed wall
The membrane is rigid and unchanging
The membrane has no proteins in it
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes a flexible sheet with proteins drifting through it. A wall-and-gates image gets the selectivity right but the rigidity badly wrong.

questions.stem: A cell's mitochondria are disabled. Which process continues for a short time?
options: Diffusion of substances across the membrane
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive and needs no energy from the cell. Active transport, protein synthesis and division all depend on energy from respiration.

questions.stem: Two cells have the same volume but one has many internal folded membranes. What does this suggest?
options: It carries out more reactions that happen on membrane surfaces
questions.explanation: Folding packs more membrane area into the same volume, which suits cells doing a lot of membrane-based chemistry.

questions.stem: Why is the claim 'plants get their food from the soil' incorrect?
options: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; soil supplies water and minerals
Plants do not need soil at all
Plants absorb glucose directly through their roots
questions.explanation: Minerals from soil are needed for growth, but they are not food in the energy sense. The carbon in a plant's mass comes mainly from carbon dioxide in the air.

questions.stem: Which experimental result would best support the claim that chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis?
options: Plants grow taller in light than in darkness
Chloroplasts are visible under a microscope
Isolated chloroplasts in light produce oxygen; the rest of the cell contents do not
questions.explanation: Isolating the organelle and showing the process still occurs is direct evidence. Whole-plant growth in light is consistent but does not locate the process.
